name: Colin Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I write stock and ordering software for builders' merchants, the timber yards and plumbing suppliers, at a firm of about thirty-five people. I start the day with my AI assistant sorting overnight bug reports, then I spend most of it building features like automatic reordering when the cement runs low. I love going out to a yard and watching a manager use something I built with dust on his hands. What wears me out is the endless meetings about features nobody in the yards asked for.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm single and rent a one-bed flat over a barber's, and I play rugby on Saturdays and go to church on Sundays with my mum. My savings are thin because I put most of them into a side project, an app that books local tradespeople, which has eleven paying users so far. The pay's lower than the cities, but there aren't many tech jobs round here and I like being near my uncle, who runs a building firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That'd be a let-down for me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still useful, and the businesses that use them sensibly will do fine. At work I'd keep showing people the shortcuts. Online I'd say the market sorted out the hype, which is how it should work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be a bit gutted, because my side app was built on the idea that AI makes small builders more efficient. With only eleven users, it might never pay back what I put in. The day job's fine, but I'd be back to square one on savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the day job and keep using AI for the boring work, because it still saves me an hour a day. I'd give the tradespeople app six more months, and if it doesn't hit fifty users, I'd shut it down. Then I'd rebuild my savings, two months by next winter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Disappointed more than worried. If AI turns out to be hype, I bet on the wrong horse, a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which routine bits would AI still take from you here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bug sorting and writing tests, mostly, which I already hand over. That's maybe an hour a day. It's nice, but it's not life-changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your uncle about the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it didn't work, and that I learned a lot. He's started three businesses, and one of them failed badly. He'd buy me a pint and tell me to try again.

say: I'd say AI tools are **still useful**, and sensible businesses will do fine.
I'd say the **market sorted out** the hype, which is how it should work.
think: My **side app** was built on AI helping small builders, so I'd be gutted.
With only **eleven users**, the app might never pay back my savings.
do: Keep the **day job** and keep using AI for an hour of boring work daily.
Give the tradespeople app **six more months** to reach fifty users.
Rebuild **two months** of savings by next winter.
feel: More **disappointed** than worried, like backing the **wrong horse**.
S0.quote: If AI turns out to be hype, I bet on the wrong horse, a bit.
fieldNote: His thin savings are a **chosen risk**, the side app, not a pay problem.
He trusts the **market** to sort out hype, fitting his free-market views.
His **uncle's** failures make failure feel survivable to him.

steps.text: Keep the ordering software job and use AI daily
Shut down the tradespeople app if it has under fifty users
Rebuild two months of savings by next winter

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I'm built for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a huge chance for anyone willing to learn, and that people should stop waiting for permission. At church I'd tell the younger lads to learn a trade and learn AI, both. I'd post a few clips about how I use the tools at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I come out of this well. I already use AI every day, I know the yards, and my side app suddenly makes sense because builders need help with bookings and quotes. The team might shrink, but I'd be the one leading the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd automate the reordering and quoting features at work with AI and show the boss we can serve twice as many merchants. I'd put my evenings into the tradespeople app and add AI quotes, aiming for two hundred users in a year. I'd talk to my uncle about trialling it across his firm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. A little nervous about money, but it's the good kind of nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues who don't keep up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them, honestly, and I'd teach anyone who asks. But I don't think a firm owes people a job if they won't learn, and that's hard to say out loud. It's what I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got less than a month saved. Isn't putting evenings into the app a risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's time, not money. I'd keep the salary coming. If the app works, it's my way out of lower pay in a small town.

I'd tell the younger lads at church to **learn a trade** and AI, both.

Add **AI quotes** to the tradespeople app, aiming for two hundred users.
Ask my **uncle** to trial the app across his building firm.
feel: **Excited**, with the **good kind** of nervous about money.
S1.quote: I don't think a firm owes people a job if they won't learn, and that's hard to say out loud.
fieldNote: He sees this world as **good for him**, so calm fits despite thin savings.
His **free-market** view shows when he says firms don't owe non-learners a job.
His **uncle's firm** is both a test market and a safety net.

steps.text: Automate reordering and quoting features for merchants with AI
Grow the tradespeople app to two hundred users with AI quotes
Spend evenings and spare cash building the app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's a lot faster than I'd want, even me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a massive shift and people need to be quick, not wait for the government. I'd tell friends to get practical skills now, because hands-on work lasts longer. I'd still say it's an opportunity, but I'd say it more quietly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my day job goes fast, because ordering software is pure thinking work. My app's at risk too, because the AI could build the same thing for anyone. The bit that lasts is my uncle's building firm, because robots don't arrive until 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right now I'd go to my uncle and offer to run his ordering, quotes and scheduling with AI, so his firm wins more jobs before 2028. I'd start learning carpentry with his crew on Saturdays, so I've got a trade for the three years after. I'd stop putting money into the app.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. I'd feel like the ground moved, but I'd also feel I can still move with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in 2031, when the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buy a couple, if I could, and run them for my uncle. When the robots arrive, someone's got to own them and send them to the right building sites. That's a business, if you've got the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the money come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the problem. I'd have to save hard for three years, or get my uncle to back me. I'd rather earn it than ask the government for anything.

say: I'd say people must be **quick** and not wait for the government.
I'd tell friends to get **practical skills** now, since hands-on work lasts longer.
think: My day job goes fast, because **ordering software** is pure thinking work.
My uncle's **building firm** lasts longer, since robots don't arrive until 2031.
do: Offer to run my uncle's **ordering and quotes** with AI before 2028.
Learn **carpentry** with his crew on Saturdays.
feel: **Unsettled**, but still able to **move with it**.
S2.quote: When the robots arrive, someone's got to own them and send them to the right building sites.
fieldNote: He uses the **robot gap** to move into his uncle's hands-on firm.
He'd rather **own robots** than fear them, a sign of his adaptability.
Money is his **weak spot**; he'd lean on family before government.

steps.text: Run his uncle's ordering, quotes and scheduling with AI
Learn carpentry with his uncle's crew on Saturdays
Save towards buying building robots by 2031
Stop spending money on the tradespeople app

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Right, that's enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a real window, and the people who move now will be fine. I'd tell young men at church to get an apprenticeship and learn AI at the same time. I'd be against big government schemes, but in favour of tax breaks for firms that train people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I can build a proper business in five years. The tradespeople app has time to grow before AGI, and by 2031 I'd want it bought or turned into a service my uncle's firm runs. My day job probably lasts three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the app to five hundred users in two years and try to sell it to a bigger firm by year four. I'd do a part-time carpentry course at the college. I'd keep the day job and save three months, because the app can't be my only bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly positive, with a bit of tension. Five years before AGI feels like a race I can win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if nobody buys the app?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've learned how to run a business, and I'd take that to my uncle's firm. Either way, I'm not going back to only writing code for someone else. That part of the job is going anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you settle down in that time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to, honestly. I'd want a wife and kids before I'm thirty-five. Five years is enough to do that, if I meet the right person.

fieldNote: He feels **in control** with five years, so the mood is uneasy, not anxious.

steps.text: Grow the tradespeople app to five hundred users in two years
Do a part-time carpentry course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, and anyone who doesn't prepare only has themselves to blame. I'd encourage people to start businesses and learn trades. I'd keep posting about how I use AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in a great spot. I'd have years to grow the app and help my uncle's firm. The second half of the decade is the bit I'd plan for, but I'm not worried yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the app slowly, invest some savings in the business, and keep the day job until the app pays the rent. I'd want to be running a small business by year five. I'd also learn the newest AI tools as early as possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and quite excited. AGI in ten years feels like a decade of opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that could go wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I got overconfident and spent everything. I've done that once with the app already. I'd keep three months saved this time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you think about where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd stay. My mum's here, church is here, and builders are everywhere. The jobs come to you if you're useful.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it doesn't give me time to build anything before my job goes. What would help is tax breaks for small firms that hire and train people, and cheap loans for people starting businesses, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the trades. Everyone thinks tech people are safe, but my uncle's carpenters will have work longer than I will. That's the bit people don't expect.

headlineQuote: Everyone thinks tech people are safe, but my uncle's carpenters will have work longer than I will.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** developer writing ordering software for builders' merchants.
He's single, plays **rugby**, goes to church, and sank his savings into a tradespeople app.
He uses AI **every day** and sees slower change as his big chance.
In **AGI by 2028**, he'd move into his uncle's building firm and learn carpentry.
He prefers **tax breaks** and loans to handouts, and stays calm when he has time.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which gives him no time to build anything before his job goes.
whatWouldHelp: **Tax breaks** for small firms that train people.
**Cheap loans** for people starting businesses, not handouts.
